findings.finding: Naive extraction of the first `#` heading may accidentally capture comments inside code blocks (e.g., `# run this script`) if an ADR is missing a top-level heading or has a code block immediately at the top of the file.
findings.suggestion: Ensure `read_adr_title()` either skips content inside markdown code fences (lines between \`\`\`) or restricts its search for a top-level heading to the first few non-blank lines of the file.

findings.finding: Stripping only the `ADR-NNN` or `ADR NNN` prefix from the heading may leave dangling punctuation in the index. Developers often separate the ID and title with characters like colons, dashes, or pipes (e.g., `# ADR-042: Migrate to Python 3` -> `: Migrate to Python 3`).
findings.suggestion: Use a regex for the prefix stripping that consumes optional trailing colons, dashes, and whitespace following the ADR number (e.g., `^#?\sADR[\s-]?\d+[\s\-:]`).

findings.finding: Executing the index refresh as "best-effort" (Candidate b) in `write_decision_drop.py` directly conflicts with the strict drift guard in AC5. If the refresh fails silently (e.g., due to a brief file lock or permission issue), the developer will commit a stale index and immediately fail CI, creating a confusing UX where their action succeeded locally but failed the pipeline.
findings.suggestion: Do not swallow exceptions silently. If the drop succeeds but the index write fails, output a loud warning to `stderr` naming the exact regeneration command the developer must run to satisfy the drift guard before committing.  Overall Assessment: The architecture of this change is extremely sound, correctly targeting the root causes of staleness and import directionality without forcing a massive front-matter migration. The findings noted are minor, localized refinements to ensure robustness in text parsing and to prevent frustrating CI failures.  SHIPWRIGHT_VERDICT: approve

findings.finding: The F3 producer is only verified to refresh `INDEX.md` “in the worktree,” while AC1 requires the ADR and index row to be in the same commit. Calling the refresh from `write_decision_drop.main()` is only sufficient if that call occurs before the bundle flow determines/stages its commit contents. A subprocess call after staging, or an F3 path with its own commit boundary, would leave the regenerated index unstaged and fail the actual requirement despite the proposed test passing.
findings.suggestion: Trace and test the complete `finalize_bundle` path through commit creation. Ensure index regeneration occurs before any staging/snapshot/commit step, and add an end-to-end assertion against `git show --name-only HEAD` and the committed `INDEX.md`, not just working-tree content.

findings.finding: Adding a second independent writer (`write_decision_drop`) introduces concurrent read-render-write races with release aggregation or another F3 invocation in the same checkout. Two writers can scan at different moments and the later write can overwrite a row discovered by the earlier writer; non-atomic writes can also leave a partial `INDEX.md` if interrupted. The existing aggregation lock does not automatically protect the new F3 producer.
findings.suggestion: Make `rebuild_adr_index()` own synchronization for the index itself: acquire a shared/index-specific lock around folder scan and write, and write through a temporary file plus atomic replace. Both call sites should use that one implementation. This retains the pure renderer while making the writing producer safe.

findings.finding: “Refresh on every non-dry-run call, including zero-drop early returns” does not define behavior when the ADR folder itself is absent. The ledger says this must not crash, but it does not say whether the implementation should create `.shipwright/planning/adr/INDEX.md`, overwrite an existing index with an empty render, or no-op. Creating a new committed artifact in repositories that have not adopted ADRs would be an unintended behavior change.
findings.suggestion: Specify and test that a missing ADR directory is a no-op for rebuild/aggregation (and does not create directories or an empty index). Refresh an empty existing ADR directory normally if that is desired.

findings.finding: The heading extraction contract is under-specified for real Markdown. “First `#` heading” must not accidentally select a `#` line in YAML front matter or a fenced code block, nor treat `##` as an H1. Prefix stripping also needs an exact boundary rule so a title such as `ADR-1040 Notes` is not incorrectly stripped as `ADR-104`.
findings.suggestion: Define `read_adr_title()` precisely—for example, the first ATX level-1 heading outside front matter and fenced code blocks, matching `^#(?!#)[ \t]+...`; strip only a leading `ADR[- ]NNN` token followed by a delimiter/whitespace. Add focused tests for `##`, fenced code, front matter, `ADR-1040`, and a heading containing only the prefix.

findings.finding: “Best-effort” F3 refresh intentionally permits the drop to succeed while the index remains stale (for example, a read-only file), which is reasonable for AC14 but conflicts with treating AC1 as unconditional. Without visible diagnostics, this creates a silent inconsistency that may only be discovered by a later CI drift guard.
findings.suggestion: Catch only expected filesystem/index-generation failures at the F3 boundary, emit a clear warning including the index path and documented regeneration command, and preserve a nonzero failure for programming errors. Document that same-commit consistency is guaranteed when regeneration succeeds; the drift guard is the backstop for intentionally nonfatal write failures.

findings.finding: AC5 requires the drift failure message to name a regeneration command, but the plan defines a library API rather than a stable user-facing command. Telling users to import a Python function or invoke `aggregate_decisions` is brittle across consumer repositories and may accidentally perform unrelated release aggregation.
findings.suggestion: Establish one explicit, side-effect-limited regeneration invocation (an existing documented script mode if available, or a minimal `adr_index.py` CLI entry point) and use the exact same command in the generated header, drift assertion, F3 documentation, and pipeline documentation.  Overall, extracting a pure renderer, retaining the legacy import path, switching labels to ADR headings, and adding drift coverage are sound and appropriately scoped. The approach should be revised to prove commit-boundary ordering and to make the newly shared writer safe and well-defined in absent-folder and failure cases. SHIPWRIGHT_VERDICT: revise

findings.finding: LockTimeout is a RuntimeError, not an OSError, so the one failure mode the index lock exists for escaped every best-effort handler. At F3 it would have killed main() AFTER the drop was written, failing the whole finalize bundle; in aggregate() it would have aborted a release pass whose aggregation had already succeeded, under a message naming the wrong lock.

Hand-rolled tmp+os.replace duplicated lib/atomic_write.durable_atomic_write, the repo's SSoT, and lost its Windows protection: os.replace raises PermissionError when any process holds the destination open (an editor, the WebUI, an indexer), losing the write. Path.write_text also translates newlines, so the LF-only render was written CRLF on Windows into a committed artifact.

REGEN_COMMAND was monorepo-relative but is rendered into the committed INDEX.md header of every ADOPTED repo, which has no shared/ directory - the one documented remedy was unrunnable everywhere it actually ships.
INDEX.md is now regenerated on a branch, so two parallel ADR-writing iterates conflict; it is in no merge-reconciliation register, so ensure_current aborts.
durable_atomic_write's temp file lands in the TRACKED ADR folder that F6 now stages wholesale; a hard-killed run would leak it into a commit.
F3 refreshes on every drop but F6 staged only 'if F3 wrote an ADR spec file', so a run that repaired a stale index left it unstaged - local guard green, CI red.
_H1_RE stripped a closing '#' CommonMark would keep: '# Migrate to C#' rendered as 'Migrate to C'.
Redundant locks mkdir (file_lock creates its own parent); index lock acquired while holding the decision_log lock on two of three paths.

One test patched by dotted string rather than module object (ADR-045), and a subprocess call decoded with the locale codec. The run's own self-review had claimed module-object patching throughout - true for one test, not the other.

Found while fixing the above: the new CLI printed an em-dash to stdout, which Python encodes as cp1252 on Windows, so any caller reading the pipe as UTF-8 raised UnicodeDecodeError (an unhandled thread exception in the test run).

Exposure is bounded: the cache also lacks the new write_decision_drop.py, so a stale cache is internally consistent (old behaviour, no refresh, no staging). Carried as an explicit post-merge action.
